summary: On the third day Esther puts on her glory and walks through the doors to the throne — leaning on one maid, her train carried by another, 'a mind full of anguish' hidden behind a rosy face. The king looks up with burning eyes; the queen collapses. 'And God changed the king's spirit into mildness': he leaps from the throne, holds her up, and says the words the scene exists for — 'What is the matter, Esther? I am thy brother, fear not. Thou shalt not die.'
whyItMatters: The Hebrew book crosses this threshold in two verses; the Greek addition slows it to a heartbeat and tells you exactly where the miracle happens: 'God changed the king's spirit.' Courage, terror, and divine intervention are held in one image — the fainting queen caught by the arms of the man who could have killed her.

keyVerses.text: Remember, said he, the days of thy low estate, how thou wast brought up by my hand, because Aman the second after the king hath spoken against us unto death.
keyVerses.why: Mordecai's charge before she goes — remember where you came from, and for whom you risk.

keyVerses.text: But she with a rosy colour in her face, and with gracious and bright eyes, hid a mind full of anguish, and exceeding great fear.
keyVerses.why: Courage defined: not the absence of fear, but its concealment in service of a mission.

keyVerses.text: And God changed the king's spirit into mildness, and all in haste and in fear he leaped from his throne, and holding her up in his arms, till she came to herself, caressed her.
keyVerses.why: The addition's theological center: the heart of the king is turned by God — the sentence the Hebrew book never writes.

keyVerses.text: Thou shalt not die: for this law is not made for thee, but for all others.
keyVerses.why: The death-law suspended by a word of tenderness — the gospel pattern of the strong stooping to the trembling.

questions.question: Who is speaking in verse 1 — 'no doubt but he was Mardochai'?
questions.answer: The Greek narrator, in an aside. The Hebrew story leaves the messenger unnamed; this translator's aside identifies him as Mordecai and adds his charge: remember your low estate, remember who raised you, and go plead for us. The aside is a small window into how the Greek text interprets as it translates.

questions.question: Why does Esther faint?
questions.answer: The addition is honest about the body: terror at 'burning eyes' drops her mid-audience. The Hebrew Esther never wavers; the Greek Esther nearly dies of fear and is caught. The fainting is the point — God's intervention is visible precisely where human strength ends.

questions.question: Why does the king call himself her brother?
questions.answer: 'I am thy brother, fear not' — the Persian king speaks the language of family, not state. In the moment of greatest danger, the relationship is redefined from ruler-subject to kin. It is the emotional hinge on which the nation's survival turns.

questions.question: How does this compare with the Hebrew version of the scene?
questions.answer: Hebrew Esther 5:1-2: on the third day she stood in the inner court; the king saw her, 'she obtained favour in his sight,' and he extended the golden sceptre. Three verses, no fainting, no named intervention. The Greek version stretches the same moment into a drama where God's turning of the heart is explicit.

questions.question: Why does she faint a second time (15:18)?
questions.answer: Relief can be as overwhelming as terror — she swoons again while speaking, 'and the king was troubled, and all his servants comforted her.' The addition refuses to make courage tidy: the body keeps its own record of what this cost.
